481.event_title: Finnish ski troops defeat Soviet divisions at Suomussalmi
481.event: In the Winter War, the Soviet Union attacked Finland with forces many times larger than the Finnish army. At Suomussalmi, Soviet motorised divisions, many drawn from the milder Ukrainian military district and not equipped for the northern winter, were tied to narrow forest roads, while lightly armed Finnish troops moved quickly on skis. The Finns cut the road-bound columns into isolated pockets and destroyed two Soviet divisions, though Finland was later forced to make peace and give up territory.
481.explanation: A much smaller force won by fighting in the season and conditions that favoured it and crippled its stronger enemy.
481.tie_back: The kural says even a crow beats the stronger owl by day, so the weaker side must wait for the time that favours it, and the northern winter was the Finns' daylight and the Soviets' night.
481._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of the weaker side winning in conditions that favour it, though the advantage came from season and terrain together rather than the hour alone.

482.event_title: Vasco da Gama crosses the Indian Ocean with and against the monsoon
482.event: Guided by a pilot engaged at Malindi on the East African coast, Vasco da Gama's ships left on 24 April 1498 and, carried by the monsoon winds, reached the Malabar coast near Calicut on 18 May, a crossing of about 24 days. On the way home he left Calicut in late 1498 before the monsoon winds had turned in his favour, and the return crossing of the Arabian Sea took nearly three months, during which many of his crew died of scurvy.
482.explanation: The same ocean took less than four weeks to cross in the right season and nearly three months in the wrong one, at a terrible cost in lives.
482.tie_back: The kural says acting in step with the season is the rope that binds Fortune, and da Gama's two crossings show fortune held by timing on the way out and lost by ignoring it on the way back.
482._accuracy_note: An unusually clean natural experiment in seasonal timing, matching the kural's word paruvam (season) closely.

483.event_title: Eisenhower launches D-Day on Stagg's weather forecast
483.event: Planners of the Allied invasion of Normandy needed the right combination of moonlight, tides and weather, which limited the possible dates to 5-7 or 18-20 June 1944. On 4 June, forecasts of foul weather led General Dwight D. Eisenhower to postpone the landings by 24 hours, and the chief meteorologist, Group Captain James Stagg, then predicted a brief break in the weather, on which Eisenhower ordered the invasion to go ahead on 6 June. German forecasters, by contrast, expected conditions to remain unsuitable for a landing.
483.explanation: Vast resources of men, ships and equipment made the invasion possible, but it was the choice of the exact moment that allowed them to succeed.
483.tie_back: The kural asks whether anything is impossible for one who acts with the right means and at the right time, and D-Day joined enormous means to a carefully chosen hour.
483._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's pairing of proper means with proper timing.

484.event_title: The Greek fleet defeats the Persians in the straits of Salamis
484.event: The Greek allied fleet, smaller than the Persian navy of Xerxes, took position in the narrow strait between the island of Salamis and the Attic coast. The Persian ships moved into position during the night and entered the strait in the early morning, where the confined waters hampered the larger fleet, and the Greek triremes rammed and boarded many of them. The defeat forced Xerxes to postpone his land campaign, giving the Greek city-states time to unite against him.
484.explanation: By fighting where their smaller numbers counted for most and the enemy's for least, the Greeks turned back the largest empire of their age.
484.tie_back: The kural says even the world can be won by one who chooses the right time and acts in the right place, and Salamis was won by forcing the battle into a place of the Greeks' choosing.
484._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of the kural's 'right place'; the 'right time' element is present but less clearly documented.

485.event_title: Fabius Maximus, the Delayer, wears down Hannibal
485.event: After Hannibal's victories in Italy, Quintus Fabius Maximus was made dictator in 217 BCE and refused to meet Hannibal in pitched battle, instead shadowing his army through the hills, harassing his foraging parties and cutting off his supplies. His caution was unpopular in Rome, earning him the nickname Cunctator, the Delayer, and his command was divided with his critic Minucius. After the Romans abandoned the strategy and suffered a disastrous defeat at Cannae in 216 BCE, they returned to his approach.
485.explanation: Fabius endured public ridicule rather than fight on the enemy's terms, and his patience was later recognised as having saved Rome.
485.tie_back: The kural says those who aim high wait unshaken for their time, undisturbed by the enemy's present success, and Fabius held to his course while Hannibal seemed unstoppable and Rome mocked him.
485._accuracy_note: Close to a dramatisation of calm, watchful waiting despite an enemy's present success and public pressure.

486.event_title: Napoleon gives up the Pratzen Heights before striking at Austerlitz
486.event: Before the Battle of Austerlitz, Napoleon withdrew his troops from the Pratzen Heights and kept his right flank weak, and the Russian and Austrian allies occupied the heights and launched their main attack against that flank. As the morning mist cleared, Napoleon saw that the allies had moved troops away from the heights and weakened their centre, and he sent Marshal Soult's corps up the slope to take it, cutting the allied army in two. His 68,000 troops defeated almost 90,000 Russians and Austrians, and Austria made peace soon afterwards.
486.explanation: Giving up the high ground at first helped draw the allies into the move that exposed them to Napoleon's decisive attack.
486.tie_back: The kural compares a strong man's holding back to a fighting ram stepping back to strike harder, and Napoleon's withdrawal from the heights was followed by the blow that won the battle.
486._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of drawing back to strike harder, though some historians argue Napoleon's feint was less deliberate than the traditional account suggests.

487.event_title: The young Kangxi Emperor removes the regent Oboi
487.event: The Kangxi Emperor came to the Qing throne in 1661 at not quite seven years old, and four senior Manchu advisers, Sonin, Suksaha, Ebilun and Oboi, governed in his name. Although he began formally attending to state affairs in 1667, real power remained with the regents, Oboi chief among them. In 1669, at the age of 15, the emperor had Oboi arrested and removed the regents, taking control of the government himself.
487.explanation: The young emperor bore the regents' domination for years and acted only when he was able to break it, beginning one of the longest and most successful reigns in Chinese history.
487.tie_back: The kural says the wise do not flare up at once but hold their resentment inside and wait for the right time, and Kangxi waited until he could act decisively against the man who dominated his court.
487._accuracy_note: The waiting and the timely strike are documented, but the kural's inner anger is a state of mind that the sources do not record.

488.event_title: Tokugawa Ieyasu serves Hideyoshi, then wins Japan
488.event: After fighting Toyotomi Hideyoshi without success in 1584, Tokugawa Ieyasu agreed to become his vassal and served him for the rest of Hideyoshi's life, strengthening his own domain around Edo and avoiding Hideyoshi's costly invasions of Korea. Hideyoshi died in 1598, leaving a young heir, and in 1600 Ieyasu defeated the rival coalition at the Battle of Sekigahara, becoming the undisputed master of Japan. He received the title of shogun in 1603, founding the Tokugawa shogunate.
488.explanation: Ieyasu bowed to a stronger rival for more than a decade and moved only when that rival's power had passed.
488.tie_back: The kural advises bearing with one's foes, even showing them deference, until their time runs out, and Ieyasu's long service to Hideyoshi ended in his own supremacy.
488._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of outward deference while awaiting the rival's decline, though Ieyasu's victory came against Hideyoshi's successors rather than Hideyoshi himself.

489.event_title: American envoys accept Napoleon's offer of all Louisiana
489.event: President Thomas Jefferson's envoys, Robert Livingston and James Monroe, were authorised to pay up to 10 million dollars for New Orleans and West Florida. On 11 April 1803, the French unexpectedly offered the whole Louisiana Territory, and although this went beyond their instructions, the envoys agreed without waiting the months needed to consult Washington. The treaty, dated 30 April 1803, transferred about 827,000 square miles for 15 million dollars, roughly doubling the size of the United States.
489.explanation: A chance that arose from Napoleon's sudden change of plans was seized at once and transformed the future of the United States.
489.tie_back: The kural says that when a rare opportunity comes, one must at once do the deed that would otherwise be impossible, and the envoys closed the deal before the opportunity could vanish.
489._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation: an unexpected, unrepeatable chance seized on the spot to achieve what had seemed out of reach.

490.event_title: Muhammad Ali's rope-a-dope in the Rumble in the Jungle
490.place: Kinshasa, Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo)
490.event: Muhammad Ali, a heavy underdog, fought the unbeaten heavyweight champion George Foreman in Kinshasa. For several rounds Ali leaned on the ropes, blocking and absorbing Foreman's punches in the tactic he called the rope-a-dope, and by the middle rounds Foreman was visibly tiring. In the eighth round Ali came off the ropes with a rapid combination that knocked Foreman down, and he was counted out, giving Ali back the world heavyweight title.
490.explanation: Ali's long stillness on the ropes looked like weakness but was the preparation for one sudden, decisive attack.
490.tie_back: The kural says to stand still like the heron while the time is not ripe and strike like its beak when it is, and Ali waited on the ropes until Foreman was spent and then struck once, decisively.
490._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the heron's patient stillness followed by a swift, decisive strike.
